claim: After viewing thousands of images, each only once and only for a few seconds, humans can determine with high accuracy the specific images that they have viewed.
source: For example, after viewing thousands of images, each only once and only for a few seconds, we can determine with high accuracy the specific images that we have viewed (Brady et al., 2008; Standing, 1973).
evidence: Supported by citations to Brady et al., 2008 and Standing, 1973

claim: Humans can remember not just the objects they've seen, but also the specific configurations and contexts they saw them in.
source: Additionally, we can remember not just the objects that we've seen, but also the specific configurations and contexts we saw them in (Brady et al., 2008), suggesting that our brains store these memories with considerable visual detail.
evidence: Supported by citation to Brady et al., 2008

claim: Repetition suppression is an adaptation-like response reduction that occurs in high-level visual brain areas with stimulus repetition.
source: One candidate mechanism for signaling visual memory percepts is the adaptation-like response reduction that occurs in high-level visual brain areas with stimulus repetition, known as 'repetition suppression' (Fahy et al., 1993; Li et al., 1993; Miller and Desimone, 1994; Riches et al., 1991; Xiang and Brown, 1998).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior work

claim: Individual viewings of a novel image produce response reductions in inferotemporal cortex that can last tens of minutes to hours.
source: Consistent with that proposal, individual viewings of a novel image produce response reductions in inferotemporal cortex (IT) that can last tens of minutes to hours (Fahy et al., 1993; Xiang and Brown, 1998).
evidence: Supported by citations to Fahy et al., 1993 and Xiang and Brown, 1998

claim: Visual representations of different images are reflected as distinct patterns of spikes across the IT population.
source: That is, insofar as visual representations of different images are reflected as distinct patterns of spikes across the IT population (Figure 1; DiCarlo et al., 2012; Hung et al., 2005), this translates into a population representation in which visual information is reflected by the population vector angle (Figure 1).
evidence: Supported by citations and reference to Figure 1

claim: Following many repeated image exposures, IT neurons exhibit tuning sharpening.
source: For example, following many repeated image exposures (e.g. hundreds to thousands), IT neurons exhibit tuning sharpening (Anderson et al., 2008; Freedman et al., 2006), and a subset of neurons reflect tuning peak enhancement (Lim et al., 2015; Woloszyn and Sheinberg, 2012), and these changes could happen during single-exposure memory as well.
evidence: Supported by citations to Anderson et al., 2008 and Freedman et al., 2006

claim: A subset of IT neurons reflect tuning peak enhancement following many repeated image exposures.
source: For example, following many repeated image exposures (e.g. hundreds to thousands), IT neurons exhibit tuning sharpening (Anderson et al., 2008; Freedman et al., 2006), and a subset of neurons reflect tuning peak enhancement (Lim et al., 2015; Woloszyn and Sheinberg, 2012), and these changes could happen during single-exposure memory as well.
evidence: Supported by citations to Lim et al., 2015 and Woloszyn and Sheinberg, 2012

claim: Neurons in perirhinal cortex signal familiarity of highly familiar images with increases in firing rate.
source: Similarly, in the case of highly familiar images, neurons in a brain area that lie beyond IT, perirhinal cortex, are reported to signal familiarity with increases (as opposed to decreases) in firing rate (Tamura et al., 2017) and highly familiar faces produce larger perirhinal fMRI BOLD responses as compared to faces that are unfamiliar (Landi and Freiwald, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tamura et al., 2017

claim: Highly familiar faces produce larger perirhinal fMRI BOLD responses compared to unfamiliar faces.
source: Similarly, in the case of highly familiar images, neurons in a brain area that lie beyond IT, perirhinal cortex, are reported to signal familiarity with increases (as opposed to decreases) in firing rate (Tamura et al., 2017) and highly familiar faces produce larger perirhinal fMRI BOLD responses as compared to faces that are unfamiliar (Landi and Freiwald, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Landi and Freiwald, 2017

claim: No study to date has attempted to determine whether repetition suppression signals in IT can account for visual memory behaviors.
source: Notably, while a number of studies have investigated limited-exposure repetition suppression effects in IT at the resolution of individual-units (De Baene and Vogels, 2010; Li et al., 1993; McMahon and Olson, 2007; Ringo, 1996; Sawamura et al., 2006; Verhoef et al., 2008; Xiang and Brown, 1998), no study to date has attempted to determine whether these putative visual memory signals can in fact account for visual memory behaviors.
evidence: Explicit statement about the gap in the literature, with citations to prior work

claim: Two monkeys were trained to view images and report whether they were novel or familiar with an eye movement response.
source: To evaluate the hypothesis that repetition suppression in IT accounts for familiarity judgments during a visual memory task, we trained two monkeys to view images and report whether they were novel (had never been seen before) or were familiar (had been seen exactly once), across a range of delays between novel and familiar presentations.
evidence: Description of the experimental procedure

claim: Visual memories were remembered over a timescale of minutes within experimental sessions that lasted approximately one hour.
source: To explore the IT representation of visual memory on both correct and error trials, we parameterized the task such that visual memories were remembered over a timescale of minutes within experimental sessions that lasted approximately one hour.
evidence: Description of the experimental design

claim: Both monkeys displayed characteristic forgetting functions and reaction time patterns.
source: We found that while both monkeys displayed characteristic forgetting functions and reaction time patterns, these behavioral patterns were not well-predicted by a spike count decoder that embodied the strictest interpretation of the repetition suppression hypothesis.
evidence: Summary of behavioral results

claim: Behavioral patterns were not well-predicted by a spike count decoder that embodied the strictest interpretation of the repetition suppression hypothesis.
source: We found that while both monkeys displayed characteristic forgetting functions and reaction time patterns, these behavioral patterns were not well-predicted by a spike count decoder that embodied the strictest interpretation of the repetition suppression hypothesis.
evidence: Summary of main finding comparing decoders

claim: Behavioral patterns were better accounted for by a linear read-out that weighted each neuron proportional to the amount of visual memory information reflected in its responses.
source: These behavioral patterns were better accounted for by a linear read-out that weighted each neuron proportional to the amount of visual memory information reflected in its responses.
evidence: Summary of main finding about the FLD decoder

claim: Task difficulty was increased by reducing image viewing time from 2-3 seconds to 400 milliseconds.
source: Following on visual recognition memory studies that demonstrate a relationship between the time that images are viewed and how well they are remembered (Brady et al., 2009; Potter and Levy, 1969), we increased task difficulty by reducing image viewing time from the 2–3 s used in the classic human visual recognition memory studies to 400 ms.
evidence: Description of experimental design with citations

claim: Monkeys initiated each trial by fixating a point at the center of the screen for 200 ms.
source: Monkeys initiated each trial by fixating a point at the center of the screen, and this was followed by a brief delay and then the presentation of an image (Figure 2a).
evidence: Description of task procedure with reference to Figure 2a

claim: After 400 ms of fixating the image, a go cue appeared indicating that monkeys were free to make their selection via a saccade.
source: After 400 ms of fixating the image, a go cue appeared, indicating that the monkeys were free to make their selection via a saccade to one of two response targets (Figure 2a).
evidence: Description of task procedure with reference to Figure 2a

claim: Correct responses were rewarded with juice.
source: Correct responses were rewarded with juice.
evidence: Description of task procedure

claim: The first image presented in each session was always novel.
source: While the first image presented in each session was always novel, the probability of subsequent images being novel versus familiar quickly converged to 50%.
evidence: Description of task design

claim: The probability of subsequent images being novel versus familiar quickly converged to 50%.
source: While the first image presented in each session was always novel, the probability of subsequent images being novel versus familiar quickly converged to 50%.
evidence: Description of task design

claim: Novel images were defined as those that the monkeys had never viewed before in the entire history of training and testing.
source: Novel images were defined as those that the monkeys had never viewed before (in the entire history of training and testing) whereas familiar images were those that had been presented only once, and earlier in the same session.
evidence: Definition of experimental conditions

claim: Familiar images were those that had been presented only once, and earlier in the same session.
source: Novel images were defined as those that the monkeys had never viewed before (in the entire history of training and testing) whereas familiar images were those that had been presented only once, and earlier in the same session.
evidence: Definition of experimental conditions

claim: Delays between novel and familiar presentations were pseudorandomly selected from a uniform distribution in powers of two (n-back = 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 and 64 trials).
source: Delays between novel and familiar presentations (Figure 2b) were pseudorandomly selected from a uniform distribution, in powers of two (n-back = 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 and 64 trials corresponding to mean delays of 4.5 s, 9 s, 18 s, 36 s, 1.2 min, 2.4 min, and 4.8 min, respectively).
evidence: Description of experimental design with reference to Figure 2b

claim: When familiar images were immediately repeated (n-back = 1), both monkeys most often called them familiar (proportion chose familiar = 0.98 and 0.94).
source: When familiar images were immediately repeated (n-back = 1), both monkeys most often called them familiar (proportion chose familiar = 0.98 and 0.94; Figure 3a,c).
evidence: Behavioral result with reference to Figure 3a,c

claim: When images were novel, monkeys were unlikely to call them familiar (proportion chose familiar = 0.13 and 0.07).
source: Similarly, when images were novel, monkeys were unlikely to call them familiar (proportion chose familiar = 0.13 and 0.07; Figure 3a,c).
evidence: Behavioral result with reference to Figure 3a,c

claim: The proportion of familiar reports systematically decreased as a function of n-back.
source: Between these two extremes, the proportion of familiar reports systematically decreased as a function of n-back (Figure 3a,c).
evidence: Behavioral result with reference to Figure 3a,c

claim: In monkey 1, performance at 32 and 64 back fell below chance (32-back = 0.46, 64-back = 0.27, chance = 0.50).
source: In monkey 1, performance at 32 and 64 back fell below chance (32-back = 0.46, 64-back = 0.27, chance = 0.50), indicating that this animal most often reported that familiar images repeated after these longer delays were novel (Figure 3a).
evidence: Behavioral result with reference to Figure 3a

claim: In monkey 2, performance at 32 and 64 back remained above chance (32-back = 0.76, 64-back = 0.54).
source: In monkey 2, performance at 32 and 64 back remained above chance (32-back = 0.76, 64-back = 0.54), indicating higher performance in this animal as compared to monkey 1 (Figure 3c).
evidence: Behavioral result with reference to Figure 3c

claim: Mean reaction times on correctly reported familiar trials systematically increased as a function of n-back.
source: We found that mean reaction times on correctly reported familiar trials systematically increased as a function of n-back, or equivalently, reaction times on correct trials increased with increasing difficulty (Figure 3b,d red).
evidence: Behavioral result with reference to Figure 3b,d

claim: Reaction times on error trials decreased as a function of n-back.
source: Conversely, reaction times on error trials decreased as a function of n-back, or equivalently, reaction times on error trials decreased with increasing difficulty (Figure 3b,d, cyan).
evidence: Behavioral result with reference to Figure 3b,d

claim: In both animals, reaction time patterns led to an x-shaped pattern when plotted as a function of n-back.
source: In both animals, this led to an x-shaped pattern in the mean reaction times on familiar trials when plotted as a function of n-back.
evidence: Summary of behavioral result

claim: The x-shaped reaction time patterns differ from patterns reported for tasks well-accounted for by the standard drift diffusion model.
source: The x-shaped patterns that we observed differ from the patterns reported for tasks that are well-accounted for by the standard drift diffusion model (DDM) of decision making, such as the dot-motion-direction task (Gold and Shadlen, 2007).
evidence: Comparison to prior work with citation

claim: The standard DDM predicts that reaction times will be matched on correct and error trials.
source: However, reaction times on error trials decreased with n-back whereas the standard DDM predicts that reaction times will be matched on correct and error trials (and thus reaction times on error trials should increase with n-back as well).
evidence: Statement about model predictions

claim: The x-shaped reaction time patterns can be captured by a simple, low-parameter extension to the signal detection theory framework, as proposed by strength theory.
source: We have, however, determined that these x-shaped reaction time patterns can be captured by a very simple, low-parameter extension to the signal detection theory framework, as proposed by 'strength theory' (Murdock, 1985; Norman and Wickelgren, 1969).
evidence: Statement about model fit with citations

claim: Strength theory proposes that a noisy internal variable (memory strength) is compared to a criterion to determine whether an image is novel or familiar.
source: Like signal detection theory, strength theory proposes that a noisy internal variable ('memory strength') is compared to a criterion to determine whether an image is novel or familiar (Figure 4, left).
evidence: Description of theoretical framework with reference to Figure 4

claim: Strength theory predicts that during a visual memory task, reaction times will be inversely related to the distance of the memory strength variable from the criterion.
source: Strength theory also predicts that during a visual memory task, reaction times will be inversely related to the distance of this variable from the criterion, loosely analogous to a process in which increased certainty produces faster responses (Figure 4, middle).
evidence: Description of theoretical framework with reference to Figure 4

claim: Neural responses were recorded from IT using multi-channel probes acutely lowered before the beginning of each session.
source: As monkeys performed this task, we recorded neural responses from IT using multi-channel probes acutely lowered before the beginning of each session.
evidence: Description of recording methods

claim: The resulting data set included 15 sessions for monkey 1 (n = 403 units), and 12 sessions for monkey 2 (n = 396 units).
source: The resulting data set included 15 sessions for monkey 1 (n = 403 units), and 12 sessions for monkey 2 (n = 396 units).
evidence: Description of data set

claim: Both monkeys performed many hundreds of trials during each session (~600–1000, corresponding to ~300–500 images each repeated twice).
source: Both monkeys performed many hundreds of trials during each session (~600–1000, corresponding to ~300–500 images each repeated twice).
evidence: Description of behavioral data

claim: The grand mean firing rate response of all 799 units reveals a fairly systematic decrement in the response with repetition that diminished with time since the novel presentation.
source: This plot reveals a fairly systematic decrement in the response with repetition that diminished with time since the novel presentation.
evidence: Description of neural result shown in Figure 5a

claim: Immediate stimulus repetition resulted in a decrement in the response of approximately 11%.
source: Consistent with a visual memory signal that degrades (or forgets) with time, immediate stimulus repetition resulted in a decrement in the response of ~11% and suppression magnitudes decreased systematically with n-back.
evidence: Quantification of neural result

claim: Suppression magnitudes decreased systematically with n-back.
source: Consistent with a visual memory signal that degrades (or forgets) with time, immediate stimulus repetition resulted in a decrement in the response of ~11% and suppression magnitudes decreased systematically with n-back.
evidence: Description of neural result

claim: Repetition suppression was stronger in the monkey that was better at the task (monkey 2).
source: Also, qualitatively consistent with the repetition suppression hypothesis was the finding that when the same analysis was isolated to the units recorded from each monkey individually, repetition suppression was stronger in the monkey that was better at the task (monkey 2; Figure 5c–d).
evidence: Comparison of neural results between monkeys with reference to Figure 5c-d

claim: A spike count classifier (SCC) is an instantiation of the strictest form of the repetition suppression hypothesis in that it differentiated novel versus familiar responses based on the total number of spikes across the IT population.
source: The first, a spike count classifier (SCC), is an instantiation of the strictest form of the repetition suppression hypothesis in that it differentiated novel versus familiar responses based on the total number of spikes across the IT population (i.e. every unit in the population received a weight of 1).
evidence: Description of decoder method

claim: A Fisher Linear Discriminant (FLD) is an extension of the SCC that allows for IT units to be differentially weighted and allows for weights to be positive as well as negative.
source: The second, a Fisher Linear Discriminant (FLD), is an extension of the SCC that allows for IT units to be differentially weighted and allows for weights to be positive as well as negative (corresponding to repetition suppression and enhancement, respectively).
evidence: Description of decoder method

claim: The FLD neural prediction at each n-back was well-aligned with behavior, including high performance for familiar images presented at low n-back.
source: This analysis revealed a high degree of alignment between the neural prediction at each n-back and behavior, including high performance for familiar images presented at low n-back, performance at mid-range n-back that fell off with a similar sensitivity, and performance at the longest n-back (64) that fell below chance (Figure 6c).
evidence: Description of neural prediction result with reference to Figure 6c

claim: Neural predictions for novel images were well-aligned with the monkeys' behavioral reports.
source: Similarly, neural predictions for novel images were well-aligned with the monkeys' behavioral reports (Figure 6c, 'N').
evidence: Description of neural prediction result with reference to Figure 6c

claim: The FLD neural predictions for reaction times were largely aligned with the monkeys' mean reaction times.
source: The resulting neural predictions were largely aligned with the monkeys' mean reaction times (Figure 6f), including increasing reaction times as a function of n-back on correctly reported familiar trials, decreasing reaction times as a function of n-back on familiar trials in which the monkeys' made errors, and the characteristic x-shaped pattern.
evidence: Description of neural prediction result with reference to Figure 6f

claim: In the case of the FLD applied to the pooled data, the best population size fell near the maximal size of the total number of units recorded (n = 799).
source: In the case of the FLD applied to the pooled data, the best population size fell near the maximal size of the total number of units that we recorded (n = 799, Figure 6g, red dot).
evidence: Description of analysis result with reference to Figure 6g

claim: In the case of the FLD applied to the pooled data, prediction quality was 94% for the forgetting function and 86% for the reaction time data.
source: In the case of the FLD applied to the pooled data, PQ was 94% for the forgetting function and 86% for the reaction time data (Figure 6c,f).
evidence: Quantification of prediction quality with reference to Figure 6c,f

claim: When applied to the data pooled across the two monkeys, the best sized SCC decoded population was 559 units.
source: When applied to the data pooled across the two monkeys, the best sized SCC decoded population was 559 units (Figure 7a).
evidence: Description of analysis result with reference to Figure 7a

claim: The SCC was a better predictor of behavior than the FLD for smaller sized populations (less than 400 neurons).
source: Additionally, we found that while the SCC was a better predictor of behavior than the FLD for smaller sized populations (less than 400 neurons), the FLD was a better predictor of behavior overall (Figure 7a).
evidence: Comparison of decoder performance with reference to Figure 7a

claim: The FLD was a better predictor of behavior overall than the SCC.
source: Additionally, we found that while the SCC was a better predictor of behavior than the FLD for smaller sized populations (less than 400 neurons), the FLD was a better predictor of behavior overall (Figure 7a).
evidence: Comparison of decoder performance with reference to Figure 7a

claim: The FLD decoder was a better predictor of behavior in both individual monkeys.
source: A comparison of SCC and FLD MSE plots isolated to each monkey's data revealed that the FLD decoder was a better predictor of behavior in both individuals (Figure 7c–d).
evidence: Comparison of decoder performance with reference to Figure 7c-d

claim: The spike count decoding scheme under-predicted memory strength, particularly at the longest delays.
source: Why was the FLD weighted linear decoder a better predictor of the behavioral forgetting function? This was because the spike count decoding scheme under-predicted memory strength, particularly at the longest delays.
evidence: Explanation of decoder comparison result

claim: In both monkeys, the unit d' means were significantly shifted toward positive values.
source: In both monkeys, the unit d' means were significantly shifted toward positive values (Figure 8a–b; Wilcoxon sign rank test, monkey one mean = 0.05, p=6.8*10−17; monkey two mean = 0.12, p=1.9*10−41).
evidence: Statistical test result with reference to Figure 8a-b

claim: In both monkeys, units with negative d' were present (proportion of negative units for monkey 1 = 32%; monkey 2 = 19%).
source: In both monkeys, units with negative d' were also present (proportion of negative units for monkey 1 = 32%; monkey 2 = 19%), although from raw d' values alone, the degree to which negative d' resulted from reliable net repetition enhancement versus from noise is unclear.
evidence: Description of data distribution

claim: Very few units with negative d' had statistically distinguishable responses between novel and familiar images.
source: A comparison of the mean responses to novel as compared to familiar images for each unit revealed that very few units with negative d' had statistically distinguishable responses (bootstrap statistical test; criterion p<0.01; monkey 1: positive d' units = 14; negative d' units = 3; monkey 2: positive d' units = 75; negative d' units = 2).
evidence: Statistical test result

claim: 400 top-ranked IT units were required to achieve the same prediction quality as 800 randomly sampled units.
source: We found that 400 top-ranked IT units were required to achieve the same prediction quality as 800 randomly sampled units, suggesting that FLD behavioral predictions rely on visual memory signals that are distributed across approximately half of the IT population.
evidence: Description of analysis result

claim: FLD behavioral predictions rely on visual memory signals that are distributed across approximately half of the IT population.
source: We found that 400 top-ranked IT units were required to achieve the same prediction quality as 800 randomly sampled units, suggesting that FLD behavioral predictions rely on visual memory signals that are distributed across approximately half of the IT population.
evidence: Interpretation of analysis result

claim: Nearly all the units (759/799, 95%) produced statistically significant stimulus-evoked responses that differed from the pre-stimulus baseline period.
source: The absence of a contribution from the lower-ranked 50% of the IT population could not be attributed to non-responsiveness, as nearly all the units (759/799, 95%) produced statistically significant stimulus-evoked responses that differed from the pre-stimulus baseline period (bootstrap statistical test; criterion p<0.01; comparison of spike count windows (−150–0) ms versus (75 – 225) ms relative to stimulus onset).
evidence: Statistical test result

claim: The ranked-SCC decoder peaked at 400 units and performed nearly as well as the ranked-FLD.
source: Surprisingly, the ranked-SCC decoder also peaked at 400 units and performed nearly as well as the ranked-FLD (ranked SCC PQ for 400 units = 91%, Figure 8d; ranked FLD PQ for 400 units = 94%, Figure 8d).
evidence: Comparison of decoder performance with reference to Figure 8d

claim: Within the subset of 50% top-ranked IT units, spikes could largely be summed to make behavioral predictions.
source: This suggests that within the subset of 50% top-ranked IT units, spikes could largely be summed to make behavioral predictions.
evidence: Interpretation of decoder comparison result

claim: Addition of bottom-ranked units had no impact on the ranked-FLD.
source: What happens when the 50% bottom-ranked units are added to each type of decoder? Addition of bottom-ranked units had no impact on the ranked-FLD (Figure 8c right, 'All units').
evidence: Description of analysis result with reference to Figure 8c

claim: The FLD largely disregards the lower 50% ranked units when making behavioral predictions.
source: This suggests that the FLD largely disregards the lower 50% ranked units when making behavioral predictions.
evidence: Interpretation of analysis result

claim: The introduction of the lower 50% ranked units detrimentally impacted ranked-SCC behavioral predictions.
source: In contrast, the introduction of the lower 50% ranked units detrimentally impacted ranked-SCC behavioral predictions (ranked SCC PQ for best 50% of units = 91%; for all units = 76%; Figure 8d, right).
evidence: Description of analysis result with reference to Figure 8d

claim: Better FLD as compared to SCC behavioral predictions could largely be attributed to the FLD preferentially weighting the neurons with the strongest visual memory signals.
source: Returning to the two scenarios presented at the beginning of this section, these results suggest that better FLD as compared to SCC behavioral predictions could largely be attributed to the FLD preferentially weighting the neurons with the strongest (by way of longest lasting) visual memory signals, as opposed to the inability of the SCC to appropriately weight reliable, mixed sign modulation (i.e. mixtures of repetition suppression and enhancement).
evidence: Interpretation of analysis results

claim: Largely accurate behavioral predictions could be attributed to approximately 50% of IT units whose memory signals were reflected as repetition suppression.
source: Together, these results suggest that largely accurate behavioral predictions could be attributed to ~50% of IT units whose memory signals were reflected as repetition suppression, and within this top-ranked subpopulation, spike counts could largely be summed.
evidence: Summary of analysis results

claim: While the lower ranked units had a detrimental impact on the ability of the spike count decoder to produce accurate behavioral predictions, a weighted linear decoder largely disregarded these otherwise confounding responses.
source: These results also show that while the lower ranked units had a detrimental impact on the ability of the spike count decoder to produce accurate behavioral predictions, a weighted linear decoder largely disregarded these otherwise confounding responses.
evidence: Summary of analysis results

claim: Visual selectivity resulted in a substantial increase in the number of units required to account for behavioral performance within the FLD decoding scheme.
source: These results suggest that visual selectivity resulted in a substantial increase in the number of units required to account for behavioral performance within the FLD decoding scheme.
evidence: Interpretation of simulation results

claim: At least two factors combined to determine that a large number of FLD decoded IT units (~800) were required to accurately predict single-exposure behavioral performance.
source: In sum, at least two factors combined to determine that a large number of FLD decoded IT units (~800) were required to accurately predict single-exposure behavioral performance.
evidence: Summary of factors affecting population size

claim: The visual memory signals that combined to produce largely accurate behavioral predictions were limited to approximately 50% of the IT population.
source: First, the visual memory signals that combined to produce largely accurate behavioral predictions were limited to ~50% of the IT population.
evidence: Summary of factor affecting population size

claim: As a consequence of visual selectivity, the presentation of an image only activated a subset of units, thus increasing the population size required for robust neural performance.
source: Second, as a consequence of visual selectivity, the presentation of an image only activated a subset of units, thus increasing the population size required for robust neural performance that was capable of generalizing to new images.
evidence: Summary of factor affecting population size

claim: For both monkeys, the minimal error was lower when behavioral and neural data came from the same monkey as compared to when they were mixed between monkeys.
source: For both monkeys, the minimal error (as a function of population size) was lower when behavioral and neural data came from the same monkey as compared to when they were mixed between monkeys (Figure 10a–b, red versus black dots) and this translated to better PQ when behavioral and neural data came from the same animal versus when they came from different animals (Figure 10c).
evidence: Description of cross-monkey analysis result with reference to Figure 10a-b

claim: Signal strength and population size cannot simply be traded off to fit any possible behavioral function.
source: While our study was limited to only two subjects and thus lacked the power to establish individual differences, the better alignment of behavioral and neural data within subjects versus across subjects is an effective demonstration that signal strength and population size cannot simply be traded off to fit any possible behavioral function.
evidence: Interpretation of cross-monkey analysis

claim: These results provide added support of the hypothesis that single-exposure visual memory behaviors are in fact reflected in the neural responses of IT cortex.
source: Additionally, these results provide added support of the hypothesis that single-exposure visual memory behaviors are in fact reflected in the neural responses of IT cortex.
evidence: Interpretation of cross-monkey analysis

claim: A strict interpretation of the repetition suppression hypothesis in the form of counting the total numbers of spikes across the IT population provided an incomplete account of single-exposure visual memory behavior.
source: We found that a strict interpretation of the repetition suppression hypothesis in the form of counting the total numbers of spikes across the IT population provided an incomplete account of single-exposure visual memory behavior (Figure 7), whereas a weighted linear read-out of IT provided reasonably accurate predictions of the rates of forgetting as a function of time (Figure 6c, Figure 7e), as well as mean reaction time patterns (Figure 6f; Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Summary of main finding with references to figures

claim: A weighted linear read-out of IT provided reasonably accurate predictions of the rates of forgetting as a function of time.
source: We found that a strict interpretation of the repetition suppression hypothesis in the form of counting the total numbers of spikes across the IT population provided an incomplete account of single-exposure visual memory behavior (Figure 7), whereas a weighted linear read-out of IT provided reasonably accurate predictions of the rates of forgetting as a function of time (Figure 6c, Figure 7e), as well as mean reaction time patterns (Figure 6f; Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Summary of main finding with references to figures

claim: Behavioral predictions could be attributed to IT visual memory signals that were reflected as repetition suppression and were intermingled with visual selectivity, but only when combined across the most sensitive 50% of IT units.
source: Additionally, behavioral predictions could be attributed to IT visual memory signals that were reflected as repetition suppression (Figure 8) and were intermingled with visual selectivity (Figure 9), but only when combined across the most sensitive 50% of IT units (Figure 8c–d).
evidence: Summary of main finding with references to figures

claim: The net repetition suppression observed is qualitatively consistent with earlier reports.
source: Our study was focused on changes in IT that follow a single image exposure, and the net repetition suppression that we observed is qualitatively consistent with earlier reports (Fahy et al., 1993; Li et al., 1993; Miller and Desimone, 1994; Riches et al., 1991; Xiang and Brown, 1998).
evidence: Comparison to prior work with citations

claim: Net repetition suppression has been reported following exposure of IT neurons to the same images hundreds or thousands of times.
source: Net repetition suppression has also been reported following exposure of IT neurons to the same images hundreds or thousands of times (Anderson et al., 2008; Baker et al., 2002; Freedman et al., 2006; Lim et al., 2015; Meyer et al., 2014; Woloszyn and Sheinberg, 2012).
evidence: Statement about prior work with citations

claim: The suppression observed was transient (~5 min), whereas the suppression that follows many repeated image exposures is much longer lasting.
source: However, the suppression that we observed was transient (~5 min), whereas the suppression that follows many repeated image exposures is much longer lasting.
evidence: Comparison of current results to prior work

claim: No evidence was found that net repetition enhancement contributed to behavioral predictions.
source: In our study, we found no evidence that net repetition enhancement contributed to behavioral predictions.
evidence: Statement about findings

claim: Following many repeated exposures, neurons in perirhinal cortex exhibit repetition suppression.
source: In contrast, following a limited number of exposures, neurons in a region now attributed to perirhinal cortex have been reported to exhibit repetition suppression (Li et al., 1993; Miller et al., 1991).
evidence: Statement about prior work with citations

claim: When monkeys are engaged in a task that involves both stimulus repetition and a same/different judgment, heterogeneous combinations of repetition enhancement and suppression are observed in IT and perirhinal cortex.
source: Notably, when monkeys are engaged in a task that involves both stimulus repetition as well as a same/different judgment about repeated stimuli, heterogeneous combinations of repetition enhancement and suppression are observed in IT and perirhinal cortex (Miller and Desimone, 1994; Pagan et al., 2013; Vogels and Orban, 1994).
evidence: Statement about prior work with citations

claim: The task a subject is engaged in at the time of viewing will have an impact on what will be remembered.
source: In fact, considerable evidence supports the notion that the task a subject is engaged in at the time of viewing will have an impact on what will be remembered (reviewed by Chun and Turk-Browne, 2007).
evidence: Statement about prior work with citation

claim: Poorer performance of monkey 1 in this task may reflect divided attention between the visual image and the targets.
source: In our study, the targets were present at stimulus onset for the first monkey but delayed until the go cue (400 ms) in the second animal, and poorer performance of monkey one in this task may reflect divided attention between the visual image and the targets.
evidence: Speculation about behavioral difference

claim: One implication of our results is that near-single unit resolution is required to determine how to appropriately weight IT units to account for single-exposure visual memory behaviors.
source: For example, one implication of our results is that near-single unit resolution is required to determine how to appropriately weight IT units to account for single-exposure visual memory behaviors.
evidence: Interpretation of results

claim: Measures that average the responses across large numbers of neurons result in an information loss that cannot fully be recovered.
source: In contrast, measures that average the responses across large numbers of neurons result in an information loss that cannot fully be recovered (e.g. via a multi-voxel pattern analysis).
evidence: Inference about methodological implications

claim: The consistent positive sign of the linear weights recovered across IT units suggests that results cannot be accounted for by motor responses.
source: The consistent (positive) sign of the linear weights recovered across IT units suggests that our results cannot be accounted for by motor responses, as the task required the monkeys to saccade to two different targets to report novel versus familiar predictions and a motor account would require that all the IT neurons were tuned for the same target (e.g. 'upward' for monkey one and 'downward' for monkey 2).
evidence: Argument against alternative explanation

claim: Visual memory signals are reflected as repetition suppression in the majority of IT units.
source: Our results suggest that visual memory signals are reflected as repetition suppression in the majority of IT units and that reports of whether an image has been seen before can be predicted by counting the numbers of spikes across the top half of the repetition suppressed IT subpopulation (Figure 8e).
